title: Tadpoles
author: Chris O’Brien
summary: Chris O'Brien uses his five-year-old daughter's struggle to remember the word tadpoles as a small case study in retrieval practice and spaced practice. Over several days she failed to recall it at breakfast, partly recalled it, and finally produced it unprompted, even demanding to be asked. He argues that she did not learn the word at any single exposure but through the accumulation of retrieval attempts, and that difficulty in retrieval is the mechanism of learning, not evidence of its failure. He then applies this to classrooms, where a word taught once and missed on an exit ticket is wrongly blamed on attention, scaffolding or learning styles. His prescription is simple: ask the question again, three days later, then a week later.
points: Learning arrives through repeated retrieval attempts across time, not through the first explanation or confident repetition.
The testing effect and spaced practice mean that struggle during recall is how memory consolidates.
A teacher who teaches a word once and never asks students to retrieve it should suspect the instruction, not the students.
Re-hearing a word is not the same as producing it from memory, just as re-reading notes is not being tested.
Schedule re-asking at three days, then a week, then again, which needs no special program.
quotes: Cognitive scientists call it the testing effect — the well-established finding that retrieving information from memory strengthens it more than re-reading or re-exposure. Spaced practice — returning to the same material across multiple sessions with time in between — produces dramatically more durable learning than massed practice in a single sitting. The difficulty of the retrieval is not a sign that learning isn’t happening. It is the mechanism by which learning happens.

She learned it somewhere in the accumulation of all of those attempts. In the struggle before the retrieval. In the gap between the swim class and the car. In the moment her brain went looking for the word and found it waiting.

A teacher introduces a vocabulary word. Students repeat it. The teacher moves on. Two days later the word appears on an exit ticket and half the class can’t produce it. The teacher concludes the students weren’t paying attention, or didn’t care, or need more scaffolding, or have a different learning style.

The research on vocabulary acquisition is unambiguous. Students need multiple exposures across multiple sessions with active retrieval in between. Not re-teaching. Retrieving. The difference between hearing a word again and being asked to produce it from memory is the difference between re-reading your notes and being tested on them.

This is not a complicated idea. It does not require a special program or a curriculum adoption or a professional development series. It requires understanding how memory actually works — and organizing instruction around that understanding rather than around the intuition that explaining something clearly once should be sufficient.
We know how to produce that moment. The science has been clear for decades. We just have to be willing to teach the way learning actually works instead of the way it feels like it should.
